Abstract
The rapid expansion of the Web of Things (WoT) and the Internet of Things (IoT) has 
raised security issues, with Denial of Service (DoS) attacks becoming increasingly preva­
lent. So, the aim of this study is to identify the security concerns in the four architectural 
layers of the Web of Things, particularly DoS attacks. For this study, existing literature are 
identified using search queries, and approximately 80 of relevant primary papers published 
in the recent decade are obtained after a thorough review which helps in addressing our 
research questions. After finding the relevant primary studies, we applied strict quality 
evaluation criteria to verify that all studies are evaluated. In addition, a taxonomy of deep 
learning (DL) techniques is presented on the basis of literature analysis conducted in this 
research, which is then used to characterize the various security concerns that occur in 
IoT and WoT systems. The study also examines which DL approaches are used to detect 
DoS/DDoS attacks in IoT and WoT. Our findings indicate that the optimal form of Intru­
sion Detection System (IDS) for dealing with DoS attacks is a hybrid IDS, which uses 
both the signature-based and the anomaly-based IDS. Moreover, DL techniques such as, 
CNNs and LSTMs, produced excellent results but are still in the development stage in 
terms of scalability and practical use. This review further highlights the present state of 
security mechanisms and sets the basis for future research, with an emphasis on refining 
DL-based techniques and improving the scalability and adaptability of security systems 
for WoT networks.

1  Introduction
Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical objects, home appliances, vehicles, and 
other miscellaneous devices that are equipped with sensors, software, and made online 
connections to gather and exchange data. IoT ensures interaction and cooperation among 
interconnected things to achieve shared computational goals (Perwej et al. 2019). With the 
expansion of wireless networks, IoT has emerged a growing part of our daily lives. As we 
surround ourselves with an increasing variety of objects, IoT development faces a signifi­
cant challenge like dealing with heterogeneous software and proprietary interfaces (Perwej 
et al. 2019). With the rising complexity and variety of IoT devices, the moniker “Web of 
Things” (WoT) has arisen as a more appropriate thought, focusing on the integration of IoT 
devices with the web and enabling a more seamless interaction between humans and devices 
(Mathew et al. 2013). WoT is the integration of these objects into the existing web, using 
development tools, application programming interfaces, and web protocols. While IoT 
focuses on integrating everyday objects using a unique addressable method at the Network 
layer, WoT takes it a step further by integrating things with the application layer of the web.

is driven by the need for a more standardized, scalable, and secure architecture that can 
support the increasing number of apps and devices. During the IoT phase, sensors, smart-

and Anees 2021). In the IoT phase, various devices such as sensors, RFID tags, actuators, 
and smartphones are created and connected to the internet (Mathew et al. 2011). These 
devices are allocated distinct addresses using addressing methods, which facilitates con­

phase, IoT devices collect data from their surroundings and transmit it to the Internet using

on-premises computers using big data analytics tools and various techniques of machine 
learning (Gulia and Chahal 2020).
This process helps to filter out important insight and knowledge from the data. APIs

In WoT, four architecture layers are involved to ensure a seamless communication 
between two devices and other existing online services. These layers assist to standardize 
how data is accessible, exchanged, constructed, and discovered, resulting in an efficient 
framework for IoT systems to function on the web. Consequently, the first layer of acces­
sibility of WoT is responsible for linking physical IoT devices to the internet through one of 
the available web protocols namely CoAP, REST, HTTP and REST API. Second findability 
layer ensures that your “Thing” is not just easily accessible to other HTTP clients, but it 
may be found and utilized automatically by the other WoT apps as well. The idea here is to 
utilize web semantic standards to establish items as well as services. This allows for the dis­
covery of things using search engines and other online directories, as well as the automatic 
development of user interfaces or tools for communicating with Things. Third share layer 
specifies how to communicate data created by objects over the Web efficiently and securely. 
The other web protocols can also be beneficial here (Laaychi et al. 2022). The last layer of 
the WoT architecture is compose layer. This layer links users to the WoT environment and 
the goal of this ultimate layer is to combine the objects’ services and data into the high-level 
web, making it easier to create applications using virtual objects and web services(Parwej 
et al. 2019). Unlike Open System Interconnection (OSI), the WoT architecture is made up 
of multiple layers that provide functionality, as seen in Fig. 3.
The proposed environment of WoT is an emerging network of smart devices that can be 
accessed just like web resources, using the application layer of the network. This has far-
reaching implications, as it enables smart devices to transmit data and receive commands 
over the internet (Mathew et al. 2011). The potential applications of such an ecosystem are 
vast and varied, such as crop and livestock breeding, sales and purchasing, communication 
and media, automotive trade, transportation and shipment, environmental conservation and 
analysis, pharmaceutical and manufacturing industries, telecommunication and business 
services, medical and health care services, and so on are some examples of industries. As 
WoT continues to evolve, it is becoming an essential part of our lives, with benefits in both 
commercial and non- commercial spaces. WoT has the capacity to redefine the way we live, 
work, and connect with one another, reshaping the world as we know it. There are a vast 
range of security threats that can occur in interconnected devices of WoT as illustrated in

In WoT the interconnection of devices creates a wide range of security threats due to the

unauthorized access, where attackers exploit weak authentication mechanisms to gain con­

nificant risk is Denial of Service (DoS) attack, in which attackers flood devices or networks 
with traffic, rendering them unusable and disrupting critical services.
Also, Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack is possible through eavesdropping and manipu­
lating communications traveled between devices, compromising data integrity, and leaking 
fake data to the system (Burhan et al. 2018; Jing et al. 2014). The interdependence of these

1.1  WoT vs IoT: DoS detection
This study makes a significant contribution by addressing the security challenges specific 
to the WoT. Most of the existing literature revolves around IoT security, which primarily 
addresses local network and local resource consumption, however, the WoT aspect makes 
the environment more complex since the devices are now part of the web introducing new

a wider attack surface compared to the Internet of Things, due to adoption of web protocols 
and online services. Unlike previous studies, it presents novel detection approaches by using 
deep learning methods specifically designed for addressing security challenges in WoT. By 
exploring these novel aspects, the study provides valuable insights into securing the next 
generation of interconnected systems.
Denial of Service (DoS) detection in Internet of Things (IoT) systems focuses on net­
work-level security measures because many IoT networks remain closed and restricted. IoT 
devices operate within small local networks, where DoS attacks happen by overloading 
the network with too much traffic or by exploiting weaknesses in device resources, such as 
sensors and RFID tags. Devices in IoT networks tend to have minimal processing capac­
ity and storage space which expose them to attacks hence lead to operational failures. IoT 
detection mechanisms track both network traffic patterns and resource consumption like 
CPU or memory to detect abnormal spikes which could signify an active DoS attack. Com­
mon defense strategies against DoS attacks include traffic filtering along with rate-limiting 
methods and Intrusion Detection Systems which analyze network traffic patterns (Mölsä 
2004; Agrawal and Tapaswi 2019).
The Web of Things (WoT) creates a complex structure by linking IoT devices with the 
internet through web protocols like HTTP, CoAP and REST APIs (Mangas and Alonso 
2019). When IoT devices connect to web infrastructure through WoT they create new vul­
nerabilities that complicate the detection of DoS attacks. DoS attacks in the WoT framework 
target both the network layer and the application layer while also exploiting cloud services 
that now play a larger role in device communication and data processing. For example, 
in electronically traded WoT, DoS attacks can include HTTP flood attacks in which the 
attacker bombards web servers with excessive HTTP requests to depletion of the server or 
blocking the access of web services to legitimate users (Kumar and Ahmad 2020). This is 
unlike classical IoT, where the attack surfaces are generally limited to the devices and local 
networks.
Hence, though DoS detection in IoT is limited to simple network-level monitoring and 
resource management techniques (Mölsä 2004), WoT needs sophisticated, multi-layer 
security measures. The broader attack surface and integration of web technologies in WoT 
necessitate a focus on application-layer attacks and the need for more intelligent and adap­
tive detection systems. By utilizing machine learning and deep learning methods, WoT is 
better positioned to handle the complexities of detecting DoS attacks in this dynamic, het­
erogeneous environment.
1.2  Objectives
While the IoT has received significant attention in terms of security threats and vulner­
abilities, the WoT environment remains an unexplored area. The WoT, which integrates 
web technologies with IoT devices, introduces new security challenges that require urgent 
attention. Given the lack of a comprehensive review on WoT security, we aim to write a 
Systematic Literature Review (SLR) on the challenges of detecting security threats in WoT. 
This review will provide a thorough analysis of the existing literature on WoT security, 
identifying the key challenges, solutions, and research gaps in this area. The review would 
also provide a framework for understanding the security threats and vulnerabilities in WoT,

2  Related work
IoT has transformed how we live and interact with our surroundings, with an anticipated 
20 billion devices linked to the internet by 2025. However, this quick expansion has raised 
several security and privacy issues, making it an urgent matter that must be tackled. This 
literature aims to provide a complete overview of the security problems related with WoT 
and to identify which security mechanisms exits to address these security concerns. Further­
more, discover the DL techniques that have been used to detect security threats from the last 
decade. This related work further attempts to bridge this gap by providing a comparative 
analysis of IoT and WoT security threats, with a particular focus on the unique vulnerabili­
ties introduced by the web-based architecture of WoT.

2.2  The expanding threat landscape of IoT and WoT
IoT and WoT represent significant developments in interconnected technologies, but 
their rapid growth has introduced a complicated web of security challenges (Gerodimos 
et al. 2023). WoT employs web technologies to improve accessibility and interoperabil­
ity, whereas IoT concentrates on connecting physical devices, frequently using proprietary 
protocols (Gerodimos et al. 2023). Existing literature often addresses IoT security broadly 
(Gerodimos et al. 2023; Abdulghani et al. 2019), neglecting the distinct challenges posed by 
the integration of web technologies in WoT. In this literature, we will explore and present 
authentication and authorization issues, API security concerns, and data privacy challenges 
specific to WoT, highlighting the need for tailored mitigation strategies. The increasing reli­
ance on cloud services introduces vulnerabilities associated with data storage, access con­
trol, and service provider security, further complicating the security landscape for both IoT 
and WoT (Nhlabatsi et al. 2018).
2.3  Common security threats in IoT and WoT
Both IoT and WoT share some fundamental security vulnerabilities stemming from the 
inherent limitations of embedded systems and network connectivity. Many IoT devices, and 
by extension, those incorporated into WoT, lack robust security features found in traditional 
IT systems (Gerodimos et al. 2023; Abdulghani et al. 2019; Mohammed et al. 2020). This 
often includes inadequate authentication mechanisms, weak encryption, and limited update 
capabilities (Gerodimos et al. 2023; Abdulghani et al. 2019). This vulnerability makes them 
susceptible to various attacks, including: denial-of-service (DoS) attacks (Abdulghani et al. 
2019), data breaches (Hameed et  al. 2021), malware infections and Man-in-the-middle 
(MitM) attacks.The increasing complexity of WoT systems, with their reliance on intercon­

2.4  WoT-specific security threats: the impact of web integration
WoT devices frequently rely on web-based authentication methods, such as OAuth 2.0 or 
OpenID Connect, for user access and authorization (Malik et al. 2023). These protocols, 
while widely used and generally secure, are susceptible to attacks such as token theft and 
session hijacking (Malik et al. 2023). Attackers can exploit vulnerabilities in the imple­
mentation of these protocols or compromise user credentials to gain unauthorized access to 
WoT devices and their associated data. The reliance on web-based authentication in WoT 
significantly expands the attack surface compared to traditional IoT systems, which often 
utilize simpler, albeit less secure, authentication methods.
Many WoT devices expose application programming interfaces (APIs) to allow for inter­
action with other systems and services (Gorski et al. 2021). These APIs, if not properly 
secured, can become entry points for attackers. Common API vulnerabilities include insuf­
ficient authentication, authorization flaws, and injection attacks (Gorski et al. 2021). Attack­
ers can exploit these weaknesses to manipulate data, execute unauthorized actions, or gain 
control of the WoT device.
Unlike traditional IoT deployments, WoT often involves real-time data sharing between 
devices and users via web protocols (Schroeder et  al. 2022). This increased data flow 
expands the potential for data interception and misuse. Attackers can exploit vulnerabilities 
in web protocols or compromise devices to access sensitive data transmitted over the net­
work. Data privacy regulations, such as GDPR and CCPA, impose stringent requirements 
on data handling and protection (Schroeder et al. 2022).
2.5  IoT vs. WoT security threats
Table 2 compares security threats in IoT vs. WoT environments, highlighting how web inte­
gration introduces unique vulnerabilities in authentication, data security, network security, 
software security, physical security, and data privacy. WoT-specific threats include web-
based authentication flaws, API vulnerabilities, SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), 
and increased risks due to real-time data sharing.
The convergence of web technologies and IoT devices has created the Web of Things 
(WoT), a powerful but vulnerable ecosystem. While IoT and WoT share some common 
security threats, the integration of web technologies in WoT introduces unique vulnerabili­
ties related to authentication, API security, and data privacy. This review has highlighted 
these distinctive challenges, contrasting them with the broader IoT security landscape.

3  Research methodology
In this section, we presented how the literature review was done and which papers were 
chosen for analysis. A Systematic Literature examination (SLR) is the identification and 
subsequent examination of a succession of scientific papers based on a predefined method­
ology, with the possibility of repeating all the steps involved if necessary. As described in 
(Brereton et al. 2007), a SLR typically consists of three review phases [32] i.e.,
(1)	 Planning
(2)	 Conducting
(3)	 Documenting
Research question formulation, review procedure development, and protocol validation are 
some of the tasks completed during the planning phase. Choosing main studies, extract­
ing necessary data, evaluating study quality, doing relevant study identification, and syn­
thesizing are all part of the conducting step.In the final Documenting the review phase, 
researchers compile the review report and validate the findings. In this final phase SLR will 
be produced in the report format or paper. Figure 4 illustrates the phases and stages that 
comprise the SLR process.

therefore, most IoT devices have been designed to possess learning capability to adapt to

they also pose significant security and privacy issues. Some dangers are caused by freely 
guessable or hacked passwords, low-cost technology, and nonencrypted information shar­

4.3  Assessment of RQ3: Which are the existing security mechanisms for threat 
detection in IoT/WoT?
Security mechanisms protect sensitive information and items from unauthorized access, 
modification, or duplication.A mechanism may function independently or in conjunction 
with others to offer a certain service. Recently, researchers have proposed several security 
mechanisms to mitigate security threats in the domain of IoT/WoT in general. Such as, a 
role-based access control architecture to protect the Web of Things and manage access to 
the data generated by smart objects (Barka et al. 2015). Another solution (Domenech et al. 
2016), to deploys AAI4WoT for authentication and authorization. The WoT infrastructure 
uses SAML and XACML, while DL-IDS, a deep learning intrusion detection solution, accu­
rately detects security risks in IoT environments(Otoum et al. 2022). An interaction between 
HTTP and MQTT protocols to ensure a security mechanism for H2T communication in 
IoT is proposed in (Almazroi 2019). The study (Roopak et al. 2020) suggests using deep 
learning and multi-objective optimization to build an intrusion detection system that can 
detect DDoS assaults in Internet of Things networks. However, security mechanisms and 
mitigation techniques to detect DoS attack in IoT or WoT are limited and we can categorize 
these security mechanisms depending upon the deployment and architecture. The security 
mechanisms identified in the primary studies are discussed in subsequent subsection:
4.3.1  Types of security mechanisms are currently employed for DoS attack detection
Denial of service (DoS) attacks use a variety of methods and tools to significantly impair 
networks (Remesh et  al. 2020). However, they may be minimized by using appropri­
ate security mechanisms such as Signature-Based Detection, Anomaly-Based Detection, 
Hybrid Detection, AI and Machine Learning-Based Detection and Intrusion Detection and 
Prevention Systems. The detail of each mechanism is given below:
Signature-based intrusion detection system: A signature-based Intrusion Detection 
System (IDS) is a security technology that captures or filters packets, logged by network 
layer devices, and checks it against the database containing unique signatures of known 
attacks (Sharma et al. 2023). This type of IDS is very effective in identifying known attack

sists of centralized and distributed modules that detect both external network intrusions and 
internal network intrusions caused by compromised nodes. The system includes IDS routers 
with detection modules and firewalls, as well as sensor-like devices known as IDS detec­
tors, which monitor suspicious traffic and forward it to the routers. This technique avoids 
the need to modify existing devices/sensors and relies on cable communication routes to

4.4  Assessment of RQ4: Which DL technique performs better for DoS attack 
detection in IoT /WoT?
This section discusses typical DL techniques for detecting DoS/DDoS attacks in the domain 
of IoT/WoT. DL architectures provide a range of possibilities for solving problems across 
multiple domains. These systems can be feed-forward or recurrent, including prior inputs. 
The following subsections provides a high-level information of the used deep learning tech­
niques to identify DoS/DDoS attack and what hyperparameter and preprocessing steps were 
used by the developers.
4.4.1  What are the existing DL techniques used for DoS/DDoS attacks detection in IoT/
WoT?
Advanced IoT and WoT technologies have recently become quite popular due to their con­
nection and simplicity. However, this development has disrupted IoT and WoT systems as 
the primary targets for cyber attackers, particularly DoS and DDoS attacks. They have the 
potential to significantly degrade services, create unsecured Internet connections, and exploit 
a variety of flaws common to limited IoT devices. Previous Machine learning techniques of 
attack detection simply do not apply to these sophisticated attacks and cannot handle their 
volume. As a result, deep learning (DL) algorithms have been created to provide a more 
dependable and accurate solution for detecting diverse complex attack patterns directly 
from network traffic. Deep learning algorithms for detecting DoS/DDoS attacks in IoT/
WoT environments are classified into three major categories: Such as: supervised learning, 
unsupervised learning, and hybrid learning. These techniques are classified into categories 
based on how they manage the data, with supervised techniques relying on labeled datasets, 
unsupervised techniques detecting anomalies without labeled data, and hybrid methods that 
improve detection rates by combining the two. This category provides examples of how 
various approaches are organized, as seen in Fig. 9, in taxonomy and explained each of these 
techniques in the following sections;
a) Supervised learning:
Models are trained using a training set in supervised learning to produce the intended 
outcomes. This training dataset provides inputs and accurate outputs, enabling the system 
to grow continuously. It includes CNN, LSTM, DBN and DNN models.The detail of these 
techniques are given below:
Convolutional neural network (CNN):
A convolutional neural network also known as CNN is considered as a heart of DL 
algorithms. CNN is a neural network that uses cascading layers with differential operators 
to encode and scale activation’s. It consists of two major components: feature extraction 
and classification. The feature extraction block consists of convolution and pooling layers

classification process run by an optimized DBN model. As a result, the DBN’s activation

Deep neural networks (DNNs):
ANNs, also known as neural networks, typically consist of one input layer, one or two 
hidden layers, and one output layer. Deep neural networks often contain a sophisticated 
hidden layer structure with a broad range of diverse layers, including a convolutional layer, 
dense layer, max-pooling layer, and other distinct layers. These extra layers allow the model 
to better identify difficulties and deliver optimal solutions to complicated tasks. A deep neu­
ral network contains more layers than an ANN, and each layer adds complexity to the model 
while allowing the model to digest inputs succinctly to produce the optimal answer. ANN 
was used to prevent different risks in IoT networks and as an intrusion detection system. A 
multi-level perceptron, a form of supervised ANN, is specifically trained using IP packet 
captures to distinguish between normal harmful behavior on an IoT network. The ANN is 
evaluated against a trained IoT data and achieved an average accuracy (Janaiah 2022).
b) Unsupervised learning:
Unsupervised learning is a sort of machine learning that learns from data without the 
supervision of humans. Unsupervised machine learning models, as opposed to supervised 
learning, are given unlabeled data and are free to identify patterns and insights without 
explicit supervision or instruction. Unsupervised DL models details are given below:
Auto-encoders (AE):
Neural networks with an output layer the same size as the input layer are called autoen­
coders (AEs). An AE includes three components(Meidan et al. 2018). The first component, 
encoder is a fully connected, feed forward neural network that encodes an input into low 
dimensional space representation. Code is a lower level of detailed information on the input, 
which can be fed into the decoder. And lastly, decoder a feedforward network which recon­
struct the input from the code back to its original dimensions. For detecting DoS attacks in 
IoT, autoencoder can be used to learn the probabilistic distribution of normal traffic. When 
there is new data, autoencoder then checks whether the reconstruction error is high or not, 
high error usually means that the model is not able to reconstruct the odd data which practi­
cally is an indicator of a DoS attack. It is one of the methods of the anomaly-based intrusion 
detection systems, which consist in defining normal behavior and identifying the deviations 
as malicious intrusions (Abdalgawad et al. 2021). Anomaly based IDS uses comprehension

4.5  Assessment of RQ5: What are the gaps in the current research, and which future 
directions should be pursued for DOS attacks threat detection in IoT/WoT?
In this section, we will analyze the gaps in existing research that we discovered throughout 
the study and consider potential future directions.
Research Gaps: The current study on detecting DoS and DDoS attacks in IoT and WoT 
contexts discusses the following points that should be researched and improved to better IoT 
and WoT security. Some of the main research gaps are as follows:
Limited exploration of diverse IoT application domains: Most of the research papers 
focus on key areas of IoT applications such as smart health, transportation systems, smart 
homes and cities, and IoT security in general. Nonetheless, little research into other poten­
tial IoT application areas has been done in the literature. To fully realize the promise of IoT 
technology, there is a demand to broaden its boundaries and consider the huge world of 
prospective sectors that have yet to be discovered (Aly et al. 2019).
Architectural considerations: Many IoT and WoT security solutions fail to appropri­
ately capture the architectural features of target applications. There is little to no extensive 
literature on the deployment of security measures at various tiers of the IoT/WoT architec­
tural stack. This mismatch makes it challenging to implement practical security solutions 
that are also optimized for scalability, functionality, and IoT device capabilities (Macedo 
et al. 2019).
Standardization of web attack datasets:  To the best of our knowledge, the WoT does 
not have any standard, real-world datasets for web-based attacks. The lack of any of these 
components makes it difficult for researchers and developers to construct security models

5  Real-world applications of DL-based security mechanisms: case 
studies
In this section, we have included case studies and experimental data to evaluate the real-
world applicability of deep learning (DL)-based security measures in the Web of Things 
(WoT) environment, significantly strengthening the review process. Although a thorough 
comparison of DL approaches was given in the previous section, this section expands on 
the conversation by looking at their actual implementation, performance in dynamic WoT 
scenarios, and potential difficulties in real-world applications. Specifically, we present three 
hypothetical case studies that highlight the effectiveness of DL models in detecting security 
threats, alongside an experimental evaluation measuring their accuracy, latency, and adapt­
ability to evolving cyber threats.
5.1  Hypothetical case studies
Testing DL models is necessary for discovering DoS and DDoS attacks in WoT/IoT. To 
illustrate how well these models perform, we present hypothetical case studies that simulate 
real-world IoT environments. These test cases show the effectiveness, scalability, and reli­
ability when using the DL-based systems to discover DoS and DDoS attacks.
5.1.1  Smart cities
The design of this test case is to check the performance of a hybrid deep learning-based 
architecture that integrates Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and Convolutional Neu­
ral Network (CNN) for DDoS attack detection in the WoT smart city environment. For that 
purpose, a simulated smart city environment is prepared, consisting of smart soil monitor­
ing sensors that track temperature, moisture levels, and battery usage, environmental sen­
sors that monitor air quality, CO2 levels, noise, and humidity, and river monitoring sensors 
assessing water quality parameters such as turbidity, pH, and conductivity. Tools such as 
LOIC can be used in simulating a DDoS attack, and Wireshark Software for capturing gen­
erated traffic, which is then labelled and saved as a.csv format.
First, the normal traffic gathered from the sensors and the attack traffic generated from 
the simulated DDoS attacks are collected. The dataset is pre-processed as normal traffic was 
labelled as 0 and the attack traffic was labelled as 1, and other features such as timestamps 
and sensor readings were normalized to be suitable for machine learning algorithms. The 
RBM is then trained in an unsupervised way to extract the high-level features from the pre-
processed dataset. Then these learned features are passed to CNN, which classifies time-
series data into normal and DDoS categories after being trained.
Then the dataset is divided into 80% training and 20% testing subsets, and the model 
is evaluated in terms of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and con­
fusion matrices. The hybrid model is then deployed in the simulated smart city environ­
ment and tested for its ability to detect DDoS attacks in real time after being trained. The 
results include detection accuracy, latency, and false positive/negative rates, which are then 
recorded and analyzed. Finally, the performance of the hybrid model is compared to base­
line models to validate its efficiency for detecting DDoS attacks in smart city scenarios. The 
IoT environment results demonstrate a high level of accuracy over other machine learning

5.1.2  Smart homes
The purpose of this test case is to assess the capabilities of a deep learning model, namely 
hybrid CNN-LSTM model, in detecting DoS attacks in smart homes using WoT devices 
such as smart lights, thermostats, security cameras, and smart locks that are all connected 
and accessible through the web page. The first step in the process is to set up a simulated 
smart home, ensuring all devices are connected to a central hub that facilitates communica­
tion over various network protocols like Wi-Fi, Zigbee, and Bluetooth. After the devices are 
configured, a traffic monitoring tool like Wireshark is installed to capture the network pack­
ets generated by the IoT devices. The dataset is created by collecting and labelling captured 
traffic data that includes timestamps, packet sizes, and other relevant network statistics. The 
dataset includes normal traffic, labelled as "0," and attack traffic, labelled as "1," where the 
attack traffic is simulated DoS traffic.
Normal traffic is introduced by simulating normal activities, such as turning lights on and 
off, adjusting the thermostat, or streaming video from security cameras. This normal traffic 
is labelled "0" to establish a baseline for the behavior of the system. In the test attack phase, 
the DoS attack is invoked through a device called LOIC, which initiates an inappropriate 
overflow of unnecessary traffic in attempts to overwhelm the communication made by the 
peripherals with the centre hub. Normal and attack traffic data are pre-processed by normal­
izing the timestamps, packet sizes, and other network features to make them compatible for 
input into the deep learning model.
The dataset is divided into subsets after preprocessing and used for training and test­
ing with an 80/20 ratio of the data set being assigned for training and testing respectively. 
The DL model used is the combination of a Convolutional Neural Network and an LSTM 
network to train it. It is CNN’s job to extract spatial features from network traffic, while the 
LSTM network is used for the time-series nature of data to learn patterns over time that sig­
nify normal behaviour and DoS attack traffic. Training lets the model learn how to classify 
normal traffic from attack traffic using the patterns within the data.
After training the model, it is evaluated using different performance metrics, like accu­
racy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix. This helps in establishing how effec­
tively the model can detect DoS attacks while keeping false positives and negatives as low 
as possible. The model is then tested in real-time in a simulated environment where live 
network traffic is fed to the system. In case of a DoS attack, the model should classify the 
traffic as an "attack" and create an alert for the user or system administrator. Also, the system 
should log into information regarding the attack detected, which includes the type of attack, 
the timestamp, and the devices affected.
After a performance evaluation, which generally records the model’s accuracy, latency, 
and false positive/negative rates, the real-time detection phase is followed. In case the 
results after the first pass are unsatisfactory, retraining the model or fine-tuning its hyper­
parameters often serves to improve performance. The performance of the deep learning

5.1.3  Health care
The objective of this test case is to validate the effectiveness of the Deep-DDoS framework 
in detecting and mitigating DoS/DDoS attacks within healthcare-based WoT environments. 
Typically, such an environment consists of critical devices, such as blood pressure monitors, 
ECG machines, and oxygen level sensors that require uninterrupted network connectivity 
for real-time monitoring and diagnostics. Strong security for these systems is required to 
maintain the care and decision-making processes involving patients.
First, the CICDDoS2019 dataset, with the full range of DDoS attack types, is pre-pro­
cessed for training and testing. Missing values are replaced by statistical means, and the 
categorical labels encoded e.g., "benign" by 0, "DDoS" by 1. Selective features, while elimi­
nating sources and destinations of IP addresses to prevent overfitting, will be selected for the 
model. The dataset is reshaped into a format suitable for deep learning models that comply 
with the input requirements of both CNN and LSTM layers.
The Deep-DDoS framework is designed using a 1D Convolutional Neural Network 
(CNN) layer for preliminary feature extraction followed by a Long Short-Term Memory 
(LSTM) layer to analyze sequential data. Dropout and batch normalization layers are used 
to avoid overfitting and speed up the training process. The final dense layer with a sig­
moid activation function classifies incoming traffic as either benign or malicious. Then, the 
trained model is deployed on an IoT gateway for real-time prediction.
In this work, a simulated healthcare IoT environment is designed to test the framework 
under the generation of DoS and DDoS attacks mimicking real-world attack scenarios. At 
each arrival of a network packet, the model predicts if the traffic is malicious or benign. If 
malicious activity is detected, the system will block the whole subnet from where the attack 
was coming to prevent any further disruption in the healthcare network. The performance 
metrics of accuracy, precision, and recall are used to evaluate the model, and the framework 
achieves an overall accuracy of 98.8% in IoT smart healthcare system (Bassene and Gueye 
2021).
The expected result of this test case is that the Deep-DDoS framework exhibits high reli­
ability and efficiency in the identification and mitigation of DoS/DDoS attacks in healthcare 
IoT/WoT networks. Real-time traffic prediction and subnet-level blocking will ensure mini­
mal impact on patient care and critical device operations, making the framework a robust 
solution for securing healthcare environments against cyber threats.

5.2  Simulated experiment in WoT environment
To validate hypothetical use cases, we established a simulated experiment for the WoT envi­
ronment where various IoT devices (such as smart sensors, actuators, and controllers) are 
connected to a centralized web-based dashboard. These devices continuously send data to 
the web application, mimicking a real-world smart city setup. A virtual machine is con­
figured to generate DoS/DDoS attacks using tools like LOIC and Hping3, targeting the 
network to flood it with excessive traffic. This artificial attack scenario is designed to slow 
down the response time of the system and simulate real-life cyber threats.
To evaluate the system’s ability to detect attacks, a DoS attack was simulated from the 
virtual machine for 10 min, during which both normal and attack traffic data were collected 
for further analysis. Network traffic is captured using Wireshark or similar packet-sniffing 
tools. The recorded traffic logs include parameters such as source/destination IP addresses, 
timestamps, packet sizes, protocols used, and response times. The captured data is exported 
into a CSV file, where normal traffic is labelled as 0 and attack traffic as 1. Before applying 
deep learning, the data undergoes preprocessing, which includes handling missing data, 
handling categorized data, Feature extraction, and normalization. Then in the data model­
ling step data is splitted into 80/20 ratio for training and testing sets respectively and the 
model is fitted with SMOTE() to balance the dataset.
After that a hybrid deep learning model is implemented for attack detection. The 
Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) is used to extract hidden patterns from the dataset in 
an unsupervised manner. The extracted features are then fed into a RNN, which classifies 
the network traffic into normal or DDoS attack categories. The model is trained on the pre-
processed dataset and evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, 
and confusion matrix.
By applying this deep learning approach, we achieved an accuracy of 90% in detecting 
DoS/DDoS attacks. After training, the deep learning model is deployed in the simulated 
WoT environment for real-time attack detection. The system continuously monitors incom­

6  Concluded discussion
The goal of this research is to get a better understanding of the current research trends 
regarding the identification of security risks, particularly DoS attacks regard to IoT and 
WoT. As part of this research project, a SLR is conducted to identify all relevant works on 
security methods and gaps. We examine papers about DoS attacks using terms like IoT, 
WoT, and security detection methods. This search is concluded in September 2024, thus 
submissions published after that date were not considered. The current evaluation focuses 
on significant digital libraries, and we selected around 80 studies that contribute signifi­
cantly to identify the security threats and mechanisms.
According to the study, most of the observed publications were published in high-ranking 
journals and conferences, with a smaller number appearing in workshops or symposiums. 
The most often detected research types are "solution proposal" and "evaluation research". In 
comparison to the existing security solutions, IDS based on a hybrid approach that employs 
both signature-based and anomaly-based methodologies were identified as the most effec­
tive in countering DoS attacks in IoT and WoT environments. Deep learning techniques 
were also often employed, although practical usage and neural network extension remain 
challenges.
Like with any research conducted via search engine, certain restrictions are derived from 
the search algorithms, the extracted data, or the possibility of misclassification. However, 
we eliminated selection bias by using a variety of similar phrases and conducting searches in 
many electronic databases. Furthermore, to reduce the potential of data errors and misclas­
sification, the study applied strict inclusion/exclusion criteria.
6.1  General observations
Observations from the literature reveals that as signature-based and anomaly-based IDS 
provide effective threat detection, their scalability and capacity to adapt to new threat mod­
els are rather low. Furthermore, it has been shown that hybrid IDS, which combines both 
approaches, is more efficient in detecting and blocking DoS attacks, making it a better 
match for the restricted IoT/WoT context. It should also be highlighted that deep learning 
techniques such as deep CNNs and LSTMs improve detection accuracy, although the avail­
able research has a restriction in terms of scaled real-world testing and validation.
6.2  Academic and practical significance
This study has both academic and practical significance. Academically, it provides a detailed 
analysis of WoT security threats across its four layers and explores how deep learning-based 
mechanisms can improve security. It is also helpful for researchers working in this field, as 
they do not need to search for relevant papers manually. This study provides a comprehen­

6.3  Future directions
As the field of WoT security evolves, the integration of emerging technologies like block­
chain presents a promising direction for future research. In WoT environments, blockchain’s 
decentralized and unchangeable ledger can improve access control, authentication, and data 
integrity while lowering the risks of data tampering and unwanted access. Furthermore, 
smart contracts can help to prevent malicious activities like replay and spoofing attempts by 
enabling safe, automated transactions between IoT devices. Incorporating blockchain-based 
security mechanisms into WoT architectures could strengthen trust, transparency, and resil­
ience against cyber threats, making it a key area for future exploration.
Moreover, Subsequent research should focus on enhancing the performance and flex­
ibility of hybrid IDS models in order to address issues associated with WoT, which are 
unavoidable in WoT system due to its complexity and multilayered nature. The continued 
development of better and more adaptable safety mechanisms, together with real-world 
application of DL techniques, are critical components for effective DoS threat detection. 
Furthermore, in order to improve the overall security architecture, it will be crucial in future 
research efforts to give a deeper examination of lightweight solutions while taking into 
account the resource limitations of WoT devices.

Abstract: The rapid expansion of the Web of Things (WoT) and the Internet of Things (IoT) has raised security issues, with Denial of Service (DoS) attacks becoming increasingly preva­ lent. So, the aim of this study is to identify the security concerns in the four architectural layers of the Web of Things, particularly DoS attacks. For this study, existing literature are identified using search queries, and approximately 80 of relevant primary papers published in the recent decade are obtained after a thorough review which helps in addressing our research questions. After finding the relevant primary studies, we applied strict quality evaluation criteria to verify that all studies are evaluated. In addition, a taxonomy of deep learning (DL) techniques is presented on the basis of literature analysis conducted in this research, which is then used to characterize the various security concerns that occur in IoT and WoT systems. The study also examines which DL approaches are used to detect DoS/DDoS attacks in IoT and WoT. Our findings indicate that the optimal form of Intru­ sion Detection System (IDS) for dealing with DoS attacks is a hybrid IDS, which uses both the signature-based and the anomaly-based IDS. Moreover, DL techniques such as, CNNs and LSTMs, produced excellent results but are still in the development stage in terms of scalability and practical use. This review further highlights the present state of security mechanisms and sets the basis for future research, with an emphasis on refining DL-based techniques and improving the scalability and adaptability of security systems for WoT networks.
